content_html:
By: Nicholas Grous and Varshika Prasanna

As the incremental unit cost of intelligence trends toward zero, we are likely on the verge of an explosion in software creation unlike anything we have seen before. In truth, we are already seeing the early signs.

Thanks for reading! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

Agentic coding tools like Replit, Cursor, and Lovable are compressing the time from idea to deployment. The result is a surge in new apps, websites, and code shipped. What once required a team now requires a prompt. What once took months now takes hours.

The supply curve for software has shifted outward in dramatic fashion.

While the magnitude of this shift may be unprecedented, the pattern is not. We have seen similar dynamics before. The internet lowered the cost of distribution. Mobile lowered the cost of access. Cloud lowered the cost of infrastructure. Each time, creation surged. Each time, power laws persisted.

In software, more supply did not democratize usage. It concentrated it. A small number of platforms captured a disproportionate share of downloads, daily actives, and revenue.

We have seen this movie before in another arena: content.

As the cost to publish collapsed, blogs multiplied. Videos exploded. Anyone could create. Everyone did. But consumption did not fragment evenly. A handful of platforms captured the majority of time and ad dollars.

Creation scales faster than demand.

Which brings us to the demand question.

When supply becomes virtually limitless, what happens to demand?

There is enormous unmet demand for better tools and niche software. But it does not follow that demand will scale at the same rate as supply. History suggests there will be a lag.

Recent data shows app creation accelerating sharply, thanks to agentic AI. Engagement, however, has not risen proportionally. In a perfectly elastic world, demand would keep pace. At least so far, that does not appear to be the case.

As an oversupply of mediocre apps and duplicative tools hits the market, the question becomes: where does value accrue?

One answer is aggregation and distribution.

When feature parity becomes cheap and every startup can ship a polished product, standing out becomes harder. Brand matters more. Marketing matters more. Distribution matters more. Ad networks and recommendation engines become the gatekeepers of usage.

The content economy makes this constraint even clearer. Consumers still have 24 hours in a day, roughly 16 waking hours. AI does not change that. If anything, it increases the value of each hour. If supply grows ten or one hundred times, competition for the same fixed pool of time intensifies.

And who controls that time?

We might like to believe it is us. But when we open a social feed, a streaming service, or an app store, it is the algorithm that determines what surfaces, what ranks, and what captures the next marginal minute.

In a world of infinite creation, the scarcest resource is not intelligence. It is attention.

If you build it, will they come?

Not by default. Only if the algorithm surfaces it and the ad dollars support it.
